text: Thornfield Analytics runs a resource group full of dev and test VMs that engineers use during the day and nobody touches overnight or on weekends, yet every one of them bills around the clock. This lab builds the script that fixes that, pulling together idempotency and error handling from Chapter 1, PowerShell's Az module from Chapter 2, and the exact use case Chapter 6 introduced: automating VM start and stop schedules for cost savings.

Not every VM belongs on this schedule, so the script doesn't touch all of them. It filters on a tag instead of a hardcoded name list: any VM tagged AutoShutdown equals true is in scope, and anything else, including Thornfield's long-running reference environments, is invisible to the script by design. That tag discipline is the same one Chapter 6's compliance work depends on.

Chapter 1's idempotency lesson drives the next decision. Instead of blindly calling Stop-AzVM on every tagged VM, the script reads each VM's actual current power state first and only acts when that state doesn't already match the goal. Run the script ten times in a row and nine of those runs do nothing at all — which is correct, not a bug, and it's what makes rerunning this script safely on a schedule even possible.

This script manages a list of VMs, not one, so a single failure can't be allowed to stop the whole run. Wrapping each VM's logic in try and catch, with a continue in the catch block, means one VM with a transient error gets logged and skipped while the loop keeps evaluating every VM after it. Without that, VM seven failing would mean VMs eight through forty never even get checked.

This is PowerShell because it's an Azure-native operational task against Azure VMs, exactly the reasoning Chapter 1 taught for choosing a tool — though the same idempotency check and try-catch-continue pattern translates directly to Python's Azure SDK if a team preferred that instead. In production, this script becomes an Azure Automation Runbook from Chapter 2, scheduled to run at 7 PM and 7 AM with no human involved. Next up: building a compliance-checking script that scans a whole subscription for tag violations.
